A truncated or malformed leftover statements.jsonl makes every subsequent extract die on an uncaught JSONDecodeError with a bare traceback naming no next step. Found by the g6 reviewer, reproduced rather than reasoned about. This is a NEW failure mode g6 introduces: before g6 nothing read the previous store, so a corrupted leftover was harmless; now the read-before-overwrite step hits it on every run. The scenario is real, not theoretical, because the writer has no atomic rename -- an interrupted build leaves exactly this state, and the user's next action is to run build again, which is the run that dies. Being fixed inline in the g6 rework pass rather than deferred, since it rides the same file and the same crew; filed here so the finding survives independently of whether that pass covers it fully.

The advisory stale-tag line prints the literal FAIL prefix while leaving the exit code at zero, colliding with the prefix checks.py and render.py already use for genuine build-failing defects. Confirmed by the g6 reviewer, not inferred: one build invocation's stdout can legally carry both a build-failing FAIL line and an advisory-only FAIL line, and nothing in the text distinguishes them -- only the exit code does, which a human skimming output and a CI grep both routinely ignore. The cost is that an advisory nobody must act on reads identically to a defect somebody must, which erodes the meaning of every real FAIL in the same stream. One-line fix, ADVISORY stale tag rather than FAIL stale tag. Being fixed inline in the g6 rework pass; filed so the reasoning survives the fix.

Nothing in the routine pipeline exercises the staleness path. The g6 reviewer confirmed this by reading the call graph rather than assuming it: check never calls render.py at all, and deterministic-rebuild structurally cannot reach the path because it builds into two fresh scratch artifact directories on every call, so the previous-store read always sees nothing. The mechanism's only routine exerciser today is a human or agent NOT wiping .code-map between local build runs -- an unenforced convention, not a guarantee.

This matters beyond g6. A detector that no automated path ever runs is one refactor away from being silently dead, and the tests are its only remaining witness -- which is precisely why g6's vacuous-negative-test defect was worth blocking on. Worth deciding at triage whether some check should deliberately build twice into the same directory so the staleness path has a guaranteed exerciser, or whether the tests alone are accepted as sufficient with that limitation recorded. Not fixed in the g6 rework: it is a design question about what check is for, not a defect in what g6 built.

Evidence scripts on this run self-check their own revert with git status --porcelain, which is unreliable in this repo under core.autocrlf plus .gitattributes text=auto, and it produced a FALSE not-clean on a byte-perfect revert. Independently corroborated rather than reported once: the g6 re-reviewer reproduced it on the crew's acceptance script and confirmed byte-identity via git diff --quiet exit 0 and a matching git hash-object blob OID against HEAD, and my own Commander attack script hit the identical false negative on the same file in the same session.

Why this is worth keeping rather than shrugging off. An acceptance script that cries wolf about a dirty tree trains its readers to ignore the one signal that would catch a real un-reverted mutation, and a mutation left behind by an attack script is exactly the kind of damage that would otherwise ship silently. The failure is also in the direction that looks like diligence, which is what makes it durable.

The fix is one line and already demonstrated: compare normalized content or blob OIDs rather than raw working-tree bytes -- git diff --quiet -- <path>, exit 0 means clean. The re-review's own two attack scripts use the corrected form and stand as working examples. The re-reviewer additionally suggested a small shared helper so every future evidence script inherits the correct check instead of each one re-deriving it; worth weighing at triage against adding another moving part. CREW_CONTEXT.md already documents this exact hazard, so the deeper question for triage is why a documented trap still reached two independent scripts in one gate.

HUMAN RULING, Tommy 2026-08-08, verbatim: "middle point sounds fine, I could buy local regeneration, but if we think we can choose a stable landing zone we should." This supersedes the plan-of-record assumption recorded in gs's decision anchor -- commit the whole map tree, owned here -- which was explicitly marked pending Tommy and is now settled.

The ruling is to commit a stable landing zone and regenerate the rest locally, and the operative word is stability rather than tier depth. He accepts local regeneration as a cost he can carry; what he does not want is a committed surface that churns. So the selection criterion is measured churn, not depth in the tree.

The tree happens to be shaped for this. map/ is two tiers: a landing zone of 115 files -- map/INDEX.md, map/ids.jsonl, and one INDEX.md inside each of the 113 module directories -- and a body tier of roughly 3,815 per-symbol pages. The landing zone tracks the SHAPE of the codebase, what exists; the body tier tracks CONTENT, what it does. A body-only edit, which is the overwhelming majority of commits, should touch nothing in the landing zone. Adds, removes and renames do touch it, which is correct and comparatively rare. Committing 115 files rather than 3,930 also drops the repo-doubling objection that critic F9 raised: 115 against 3,838 tracked files is noise rather than a change in the repo's character.

What gs must do with this, and the reason it is filed rather than just noted: the stability claim above is a prediction, and this run has been burned twice by checks that could only agree with the thing they were checking. gs must MEASURE it -- body-only edit, rebuild into a scratch directory, diff, and require the landing zone byte-identical. If it is not identical the zone is drawn in the wrong place and must be redrawn before anything is committed. Repeat for an add and a rename and record what actually moves, so the churn a real commit produces is a stated number. gb already measured a rename touching 217 of 3865 pages; how many of those were INDEX pages bounds the rename case directly and that number should be recovered rather than re-derived.

The reason to commit anything at all is unchanged and must survive the narrowing: the skills instruct crews to start from a map entry point, and that instruction has to resolve to a file that exists in a fresh checkout. A landing zone that does not satisfy that has saved space and broken the feature.

The cull test is honest but low-information as a decision procedure, and that is a finding about the method rather than about g7. The g7 reviewer graded it directly: the renderer was genuinely built first and nothing was artificially flattened to dodge the question, so it is not circular -- but nothing in a flat kind-colon-text render surface would plausibly have needed a branch on kind whichever words survived, so the KEEP outcome was never realistically reachable. Two of the five words were also categorically exempt by the spec's own wording, never tested and found to differ. The decision that actually got made -- which words the corpus needs -- was settled by author-convergence data, not by render necessity, which is not what the test claims to measure.

This is the tc38 family in a softer form and worth naming separately, because the two failure modes look different in the wild. A check that cannot fail is usually visible once someone asks the question. A decision procedure whose outcome is fixed by the SHAPE of the thing being measured rather than by the question being asked still reads as rigorous, still produces a defensible artifact, and still gets cited later as though a real test was run. The cull verdict is a good artifact and its conclusion happens to be right; the concern is that it would have read equally convincing had the conclusion been wrong.

Worth deciding at triage what, if anything, this changes. The candidate reform is that a design test written into a spec should state in advance what result would falsify it and what the world would have to look like for the other branch to win -- the same discipline this run already applies to falsifiers and to disable attacks, moved upstream to the point where the test is specified rather than the point where it is run. Not proposed as machinery; a sentence in the spec would do it. Filed rather than acted on because it reaches beyond this issue into how design tests get written.

Tag staleness does not survive a symbol rename, while anchor staleness does. Found live by the g7 re-reviewer, not reasoned about: it renamed a function and changed its body in the same commit with the tag and anchor comments untouched, and stale-anchor fired while stale-tag did not. The cause is structural rather than a bug -- anchors are keyed on their slug, which survives a rename, and tags are keyed on owning symbol plus tag text, which does not. A renamed symbol therefore looks like a brand-new symbol carrying a brand-new tag, so its history resets and the body change goes unflagged.

This is a necessary consequence of the identity key the gate chose and it was chosen for good reasons: a tag has no slug of its own, and keying on the text is what makes the rule "flag when the body changed while the tag text did not" expressible at all. So this is not rework. It is a real, previously-unnamed asymmetry between the two halves of the same detector, and the failure direction is silence, which is the direction this run has repeatedly found most expensive -- the same shape as the tag mechanism not watching tags at all, which took a Commander code read to catch after a reviewer scored it as phrasing.

What triage should weigh: whether to name it in a doc line so a future author is not surprised, or to close it by giving tags a slug-like stable identity, which is a larger design move and would revive the serial-number identity machinery the design spec explicitly rejected on cost grounds while regeneration stays cheap. The cheap option is the doc line. The expensive option should not be taken without evidence that renames under live tags actually happen, which nobody has measured.

The widened dispatch-on-kind pin test still misses two evasions, and its docstring claims more than it verifies. The g7 re-reviewer confirmed both live with a standalone AST probe rather than by reading the code: getattr(obj, t['kind'], default) evades because the Call branch matches only .get() method calls and not the builtin getattr, and a locally-renamed variable before a lookup -- k = t['kind'] then LABEL[k] -- evades because the Subscript branch recognizes only a literal Name whose id is exactly "kind". Both shapes were named as candidate evasions in the original review handoff and neither is closed by the remediation.

Not blocking and correctly not blocked on: the shipped tag_lines contains neither shape, so there is no present exploit. The concern is the claim rather than the code. This test is the load-bearing evidence for the cull verdict -- the argument that the renderer treats every tag kind identically rests on it -- so a pin that reads as exhaustive while catching three shapes out of five is the softer form of the same problem this run keeps hitting: not a check that cannot fail, but a check whose failure coverage is narrower than its reputation. If the verdict is ever challenged, the pin is what gets cited.

Cheapest honest fix is to narrow the docstring to state exactly which dispatch shapes are covered. Widening further is possible but chases an open-ended set, and an accurate narrow claim is worth more than a broad one that is false at the edges. Filed rather than fixed because the choice between narrowing the claim and widening the check is a judgement about how much the cull verdict will be leaned on later.
